MRS. MACINNIS-APPOINTMENTS TO CANADIAN CONSUMER COUNCIL
speechtext:
I have a question of privilege to raise. It arises out of the announcement yesterday by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs of the personnel of the new Canadian Consumer Council. Among those named is Mr. A. J. E. Child, president of Burns Foods Limited of Calgary. To my mind this raises a question of privilege.
A few days ago I drew to the attention of this house a complaint from Calgary about a frozen confection known as fudgsicles, manufactured by the Woodland Dairy of Edmonton. On the wrapper it states that these fudgsicles contain three fluid ounces. Numerous checks, both before and after the complaint was made, have established that these fudgsicles contain only two and one half ounces. A written report dated October 25 from the Chemical and Geological Laboratories Limited of Calgary stated that their actual average fluid measure was found to be 2.516 ounces.
It is now more than three months since the complaint was lodged. Although the complainant was assured by the minister's office on August 28 that the matter was in hand and that the complainant would be notified when the report was finalized, to the best of my knowledge he has had no further word, either of the progress of the investigation or of the finalization of the report. Meanwhile, if the evidence is correct, the public is still being defrauded by the sale of these Woodland Dairy fudgsicles; and it would seem there is substance to the complaint.
When I outlined the matter in the house last Monday night the minister's parliamentary secretary stated:
While shortages in volume of fluid ounces were found to be smaller than those reported to the department, fudgsicles checked by the displacement method had volume content somewhat below declared value.
And again:
I am advised that the dairy products division will again make special checks in addition to its normal program of control, in order to determine whether the reported shortages are indicative of a current production problem or are limited to a small stock from older production.
Mr. Speaker, if the public is being defrauded it is being defrauded, whether by current production or older production matters not a scrap. Surely if rotten potatoes or bad meat were found in circulation they would be withdrawn, certainly within a period of more than three months. If these fudgsicles were found by the department to be under advertised content they should have been withdrawn from sale immediately. Instead, it is apparent that the department is allowing the Woodland Dairy ample time to sell them to an unsuspecting public.
Now, Mr. Speaker-and this is my question of privilege-the minister has appointed the president of Burns Foods Limited, the firm of which Woodland Dairy is an affiliated subsidiary, to serve on the Canadian Consumer Council, the body which is just now being established to protect consumers.
It is needless for me to labour the point. Until this whole matter has been thoroughly investigated and the complainant notified of the result, I feel strongly that the appointment of Mr. Child to the Canadian Consumer Council should be held in abeyance. If Your Honour agrees with me that this is a prima facie question of privilege, I am prepared to make a motion that consideration of Mr. Child's appointment be referred to the appropriate committee.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. speechtext:
I should like to say, based on the premise of the question, that the grounding did not result from the suggestion made to Colonel Ojukwu, but rather took place for other reasons. It took place apparently as the result of an attack damaging aircraft under Caritas

DEBATES	November 7, 1968
and under Red Cross charter on the ground at Uli. I believe that as a result of that attack the Red Cross has suspended all flights to Uli, at least until yesterday. Therefore the suspension was not linked in our minds to what we had requested of Colonel Ojukwu.

Mr. Speaker, a colleague in my party has described this budget as a colossal fraud which has the full support and blessing of the chamber of commerce. I wish to underline that statement. The Minister of Finance has taken an approach that is typical of an accountant. It is obvious that he is more interested in figures and balances than in people, human problems and human resources.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
The best example of this is the imposition of the 2 per cent social development tax with an upper limit of $120, which indicates the minister's concern for the upper income group compared with the majority of Canadians. The speech of the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell) last evening indicated his concern about the decision of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) to lessen the impact of this tax on the middle and upper income groups. In this connection I recall the statement made recently by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in Halifax to the effect that he intends to reduce the amount of income tax payable by those in the higher income brackets. He attempted to show that people in the higher income groups already pay tax at the rate of 80 per cent and that it would be unfair to impose an additional 2 per cent tax without modification.
The approach taken by this government is a simple one. It is its duty, it says, to raise taxes in order to pay for government expenditure, and since the government has increased its spending, which may have contributed to inflation, the best thing it can do is to impose taxes and create a slack in the economy. It calls this taking the fire out of inflation.
We have taken the position that there is nothing sacrosanct about balanced budgets. I recall that the late President Kennedy used deficit financing in the early sixties to get the United States economy out of the doldrums. We believe that balanced budgets are not the answer to the problems which face Canada today. The action taken by the Minister of Finance was taken in the face of a report which according to the minister's own economic white paper, showed that the rise in prices reached a peak in 1966, declined a little in 1967, and declined further in the first half of 1968. For example, there was a 4.5 per cent rise in prices in 1966, a 3.9 per cent rise in
1967	and a 3.3 per cent rise in the first half of
1968	compared with the first half of 1967.

Thus, contrary to the inflation psychosis of the Minister of Finance and the chamber of commerce, the rate at which prices have been rising has moderated over the last year and a half.
It is clear that the minister, without stating any specific policies, has opted for price stability to the detriment of full employment. The minister shows no concern for the 500,000 or more unemployed in Canada. It is true that full employment is an elastic concept and one to be achieved at the risk of some price inflation and some marginal trade-off of one for the other. But for obvious social reasons most Canadians prefer to accept a little inflation in order to obtain the full employment of men and resources, putting us in a better position to assist those groups which are most seriously affected by the rise in the cost of living, for example, pensioners, the old and the handicapped. The budget does nothing to obtain full employment or to assist the poor and elderly people of Canada.
We in the New Democratic party put people first, and this is why we would direct the economy to the attainment of full employment and increased productivity. By attaining these goals we can fulfil the basic needs of all groups in society and give people a pride and dignity worthy of achievement. This is why we in the New Democratic party support the principles and proposals set forth in the report of the Carter Commission. We do so because of the tax equity which would be achieved by following those recommendations. And this is why our monetary policies would be directed to full employment. Again, it is with this in mind that we have advocated a prices review board to prevent unwarranted and unjustified price increases such as are being imposed on Canadians today.
Tinkering with the economy by making the insurance companies pay their fair share of taxes, by making the banks, mortgage lenders and institutional lenders reduce their tax deductible reserves from 3 per cent to 1J per cent and by making the corporations accelerate their tax payments, as the government proposes, are steps in the right direction. But the refusal of the government to use fiscal and monetary policies in order to obtain the goals set out by the Economic Council of Canada, namely, full employment, a high rate of economic growth, and the equitable distribution of rising incomes, makes this a disappointing and disheartening approach to the so-called just society, especially when it is coupled with the almost total rejection of the 29180-160}

I should like to address the main burden of my remarks to Canada's most serious social problem today, the crisis in housing. There was no reference to this serious subject in the Speech from the Throne, and the only reference to housing conditions in Canada in the minister's budget statement was to the effect that the capital budget of the C.M.H.C. next year would reflect the conclusions of the government after it had received the views of the special task force on housing. It should be made to present an interim report and the government should act on that interim report immediately. To wait until the task force makes a final report will mean that no action can be taken until spring. In this connection I think we heed the slogan which the minister of labour used in his advertisements: Don't wait 'til spring, do it now!
The federal government must accept the major blame for the housing crisis in Canada today. Why has there been a housing crisis, Mr. Speaker? Why is there a shortage of housing and why are homes so expensive? The shortage in housing has been caused because this nation has not made up its mind that it wants decent housing for all its citizens. Housing should be regarded as a right and not a privilege, in the same way as we regard education. If we regarded education in the same way as we regard housing the majority of Canadian children would have a hard time getting inside a classroom.
We have also regarded housing with an almost complete dependence on private enterprise and the rules of private profit. This is why only 65 per cent of the people in Canada can take care of themselves in the matter of housing accommodation.
The solution lies in some form of social housing that is not for the benefit of investors, for the regulation of the economy, or for the purpose of making profit, but which has no other purpose than to provide homes for people. It is obvious that probably about 35 per cent of our people cannot go it alone in housing. That is why, if we had 20 per cent of our housing starts in some form of public housing and about 15 per cent in some form of co-operative housing, we would probably be the best housed people in the world. Of the 164,000 homes that were built last year only 10,000 were public and co-operative units.
The philosophy of the government, as reflected in C.M.H.C., has been a policy of letting the private institutions, the private lenders, take care of most of the home building. The corporation assumes the responsibility of providing the moneys for public and low income housing. C.M.H.C. set aside $500 million to take care of this sector but just last month we found out that these moneys were not taken up for public and low income housing and in fact the minister had to transfer $170 million out of this fund to initiate more homes and housing starts. This indicates that the policy of having the private institutions provide the money for private homes and having the government take the responsibility for public and low cost housing has not succeeded.
Why are homes so expensive, Mr. Speaker? The two main reasons are the high cost of

land and the high interest rates. The cost of land has reached prohibitive prices. In the city of Toronto the average lot ranges between $8,000 and $10,000, and this is indicative of the high price of land throughout the country. In the city of Toronto the average cost of a home is between $29,000 and $30,000. One wonders why the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen) would publish a booklet indicating that the cost of homes in Canada averages $19,000 for a new home and $12,000 for an old home. I would like to ask the Minister of Transport how immigrants in Toronto, or in fact any other person, could buy homes at those prices?
Interest rates are the highest in the history of Canada-8J per cent on N.H.A. loans and 9 to 9J per cent on conventional loans. At these rates most Canadians cannot afford the high cost of mortgages. In fact, an $18,000 mortgage at the conventional rate of 9 per cent works out at approximately $50,000 over a 25-year period.
What is the short term answer to the housing crisis? I feel certain that the Minister of Transport knows the answer. It is not necessary to await the report of the task force on housing. In the Minister of Transport we have a man who has had wide experience in housing. In fact he became a millionaire as a result of his enterprises in housing. We have in him a man of concern. I am sure he is very anxious to solve Canada's housing problems, and I feel doubly certain he could take immediate action right now.
No speech should be completely destructive, Mr. Speaker. We in the New Democratic Party tend to be more constructive than destructive. This is why I am going to suggest certain answers to the housing problem which the Minister of Transport could adopt immediately.
First, the sum of $1J billion should be set aside in the capital budget of C.M.H.C. to increase the stock of public, low rental, cooperative and senior citizens housing units and to provide subsidies to certain projects. This compares with the $500 million that was set aside by C.M.H.C. We need a massive infusion of money to take care of this problem if our goal is to have 20 per cent of our program directed to public and co-operative units.
Second would be a federal plan or target of 250,000 housing starts in 1969, made up of a mix of 65 per cent private family housing, 25 per cent public, low rental and senior citizens homes, and 10 per cent co-operative housing
November 7, 1968	COMMONS
and shell housing. The figure of 250,000 is 50,000 over the number projected by the Economic Council of Canada. When we take into account the shortfall of housing that we have had in the last few years 250,000 would only begin to take care of the present shortage.
Third, there should be an amendment to section 35A of the National Housing Act, which contains the provisions with regard to public housing. The capital costs of land acquisition and construction of housing should be changed from the present governing formula of 75-25 per cent to 90-10 per cent.
The best illustration I can give in this respect is the report from C.M.H.C. within the last few days that the city of Brandon has embarked on the purchase of land, to the amount of $400,000, in co-operation with C.M.H.C. On the basis of the present formula the federal government will pay 75 per cent of the cost of acquisition of land and the city of Brandon 25 per cent. That city is fortunate to be able to meet 25 per cent of the cost of land acquisition.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Last year the federal-provincial conference on housing recommended, in particular the provincial representatives, that the formula be changed from 75-25 per cent to 90-10 per cent. This would mean that the operating costs for these public housing projects should also be changed from the present formula of 75-25 per cent to 90-10 per cent. When one thinks of the burden municipalities bear with regard to these public housing projects in having to provide schools, fire and recreational facilities, it would not seem to be too much to ask that the federal government contribute 90 per cent of the operating costs of public housing in Canada. This is known as the cost sharing formula under section 35(e) of the National Housing Act. Subsidies in respect of low income rentals should be changed from the present 50-50 relationship to a subsidy tied in with the income of the tenants. Again this is one of the recommendations of the provincial representatives at the federal-provincial conference on housing last year.
As a fourth recommendation we would ask that the government, if necessary by amendment to the Bank Act and the Insurance Act, direct the investment of private capital to meet the shortage of private family units. The reason we ask this is that the experience of the Minister of Transport is that the insurance companies are not playing their full role in lending money to solve the housing

The Budget-Mr. Gilbert crisis in Canada. In the month of August he summoned to Ottawa representatives of the banking and insurance institutions and pleaded with them to put more money into housing. He also spoke to them about condominium housing. The answer by the banks and insurance companies was that this field had not been tested and therefore they were not prepared to invest in it. This has resulted in the Minister of Transport having to use part of the $170 million to finance condominium housing in Canada. Condominium housing provides part of the answer to the crisis because it not only creates more housing units but also gives the people an opportunity to have ownership in an apartment building and a share in all the other facilities. Many people who rent apartments and who pay high prices for them have no feeling about them and no right of ownership in the building.
Fifth, we ask the government to establish immediately a land bank for the acquisition by the federal, provincial and municipal governments of land and for the provision of services. There is nothing new about this; the city of Toronto and many other cities now purchase lands for industrial purposes. By so doing they get the money back in the form of taxes at a later date. I should like to see the immediate establishment of a land bank so that the provincial and federal governments could participate in land acquisition.
As I look across the way I think of the hon. member who represents one of the Yorks and who is a former mayor of the city of Toronto. I also think of the hon. gentleman from Davenport who at present is a councillor of the city of Toronto. If these gentlemen were to take an active role with the city of Toronto to have the city acquire land in co-operation with the federal government, then the Toronto Daily Star could not criticize the members from Toronto for their lack of initiative and lack of ideas concerning the housing shortage in Toronto.
In order to reduce the high cost of homes we also ask that the government implement the recommendation of the Carter report with regard to imposing a capital gains tax on real estate speculation. This has been needed for many months. When one thinks of the profits that are creamed off by the speculators, is it any wonder that people are becoming annoyed at the lazy attitude of the government with regard to implementing a capital gains tax? I was most happy when the hon. member for Scarborough East scorched his government and urged it to impose a form of capital gains tax.

The Budget-Mr. Gilbert
The next recommendation is that the interest rate be fixed at 6 per cent. We should realize that the interest rates are determined by the flow of money. Many spokesmen on behalf of the government say that we cannot fix interest rates at 6 per cent because it is necessary to go to the market to borrow money and that in this regard it is necessary to go to the United States. I should like the Minister of Transport to tell the house how much money we get from the United States for the construction of homes in Canada. We get very little. The flow of money is determined by the lending institutions. They hold back until they can obtain the highest interest rate possible. They also invest in luxury apartments and shopping centres to the detriment of public and private housing in Canada.
It has been suggested many times that a further recommendation should be the removal of the federal sales tax of 11 per cent on building materials. We in the New Democratic party would add the stipulation that the removal of the federal sales tax should apply only to homes costing less than $25,000. It could also be suggested that this might be connected with the idea used in the province of British Columbia where they use their sales tax as part of the down payment by a purchaser of a new home. It is very easy to assess the amount of sales tax that goes into a building. The combined provincial and federal grants would provide many Canadians, especially young people, with the required down payment for a new home today.
We would also recommend the imposition of rent controls where a city or town requests rent controls. In Ottawa the board of control passed a resolution that rent control be imposed in the city. There has been no action in this regard by the provincial government. No assistance has been given by the federal government. The federal government has had wide experience in implementing rent controls. Yesterday we heard the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Brown) recommend that rent controls be imposed in Brantford. I ask that rent controls be implemented with regard to Toronto. Toronto has one of the highest rental rates in Canada. There the landlords through associations agree among themselves on the rents they will apply to their apartments while the tenants are left to the four winds of heaven in negotiating with the landlords. It is high time the city of Toronto, with the assistance of the federal government, imposed rent controls.
The problem of implementing a national building code is very important because if
[Mr. Gilbert.)

housing is to get off the ground there is need for such a code to cut through the red tape that prevents many municipalities embarking on a housing program.
These are the short term recommendations of the New Democratic party. We have long term proposals with regard to satellite towns, transportation problems, the location of industry, recreational facilities, land use control and the ever present problem of pollution. Mr. Speaker, before coming to the heart of the matter, I should like to draw the attention of the house on the answer I received to question No. 513 I put on the order paper some time ago, and which reads as follows:
For the period October 10 to 15, 1968, inclusive, how much time was alloted by the CBC to (a) the Parti Quebecois (b) the Ralliement Creditiste, during information programs and during free programs?
The period October 10 to 15 is the one during which the Parti Quebecois held its convention in Quebec City while the Ralliement Creditiste was holding one in Sherbrooke.
Now, a Montreal newspaper, the Journal de Montreal-it is its name-wrote that we got twice as much broadcasting time as the Parti Quebecois, while gathering five times fewer people; I do not know what inspired journalist of his Montreal newspaper.

At all events, I have before me the answer given by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) who informs me that the Parti Quebecois got approximately five hours and forty-one minutes on the French networks-not only forty minutes, but five hours and forty-one minutes-and approximately three hours and five minutes on the English networks.
The Ralliement Creditiste, which held its convention in Sherbrooke at the same time, was given about one and a half hours on the C.B.C. French network, or four hours and eleven minutes less than the Levesque group. We were given about seven minutes on the English network, as compared to the three hours and five minutes given to the Parti Quebecois. In other words, the Parti Quebecois was given three hours more than we were, in order to make itself known.
Mr. Speaker, I see nothing wrong with the C.B.C. giving five hours and again three hours and five minutes of broadcasting time to the Parti Quebecois. But I do object to the fact that it only gave one hour and thirty minutes on the French network and seven minutes on the English network to the Ralliement Creditiste, a national movement with 14 representatives in the House of Commons. Our members are here this afternoon. They won their seats fairly, and the C.B.C. does not seem to take this fact into account.
It is said that Mr. Levesque's Parti Quebecois is new. And so, we spend millions of

Mr. Speaker, I have said for some years now and I will repeat that there exists notorious discrimination in the C.B.C. and the authorities should see to it that the situation is rectified. I repeat that we have no objection to periods of time being allotted, but we must not forget that they are paid by all the Canadian citizens. Why did the C.B.C. ignore the fact that, six months before the convention of the Ralliement Creditiste, we phoned their officials from my office to tell them that some delegates from all the provinces were expected in Sherbrooke in order to expand our structures. It was something new, was it not, but the C.B.C. did not take that into account. How much time have we been granted by the C.B.C. when the Ralliement Creditiste was founded? Just about fifteen minutes in Quebec. Under these circumstances, I say that the C.B.C. is practising discrimination.
Although I did say that I do not object to Mr. Levesque's movement being granted some television time, we had heard about his new party for the last six months. Incidentally, over the past six months, the Secretary of State had almost every evening seen Mr. Levesque on both the French and the English networks of the C.B.C.
At the time of the amalgamation of Mr. Levesque's and Mr. Gregoire's groups, it was reported that few Creditistes from the other provinces were present at the Sherbrooke convention. Did the Secretary of State not read in the newspapers and hear that, on the occasion of the founding of the Parti Que-becois, there were only 70 members of the Gregoire group attending? Why then is the C.B.C. treating the Ralliement Creditiste differently from the Levesque separatist movement? The Secretary of State is aware of this situation. This is discrimination.
Again, I repeat that I do not object to the covering of conventions. In the case of Levesque, the C.B.C had three cameras, one in colour, circulating around the hall of the small Quebec Coliseum that were accompanied by a crowd of C.B.C. employees. Who is paying for it? Everybody. I submit to the Secretary of State that this is not helping Canada nor is it contributing to national unity to see constantly on TV people who are aiming at the destruction of Canada instead of trying to unite it.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

It is all very well to report news, but it should not take three hours or five hours and fifty one minutes. At one time,

it lasted three hours and five minutes in English.
I will now leave that subject, but I want to remind the Secretary of State, who is now in the house, that he is the minister responsible for the C.BC., and it is not the C.B.C. which is responsible to the Secretary of State.
When I appealed to the Secretary of State, he answered somewhat on the same lines as a while ago: Does the member not accept the fact that an event may be considered by C.B.C. experts as suitable for producing a program? The experts, they are the ones who decide whether it is logical not that mention be made of the founding of a new party

that is only logical-but I do not think that millions of dollars of our tax money should be spent by the C.B.C. for the sole pleasure of having our mind poisoned through our national television and radio network.
Mr. Speaker, I think things will change one day, and that more importance will be given to those who advocate understanding and cooperation between the various elements in Canada rather than to those who only seek to divide, destroy, break up and crush, as is now the case.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make some remarks on another point, which does not concern the Secretary of State and on which I would like to draw the attention of the government. It is about the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, another federal agency. I wish to point out that there also, there is discrimination against the province of Quebec.
We made a great many requests. There are at the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation people who spare no trouble in order to study every request and give an answer.
However, let us take question No. 427 which I put on the order paper and which reads as follows:
1. How many loans were requested from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, by province during 1967?
How many loans were subsequently granted in each province?
What is the total amount, for each province, of the loans thus granted?
Mr. Speaker, although the other provinces filed some applications, I will only speak about Quebec and Ontario, the two neighbouring and largest provinces of Canada.
Quebec filed 11,108 applications and Ontario 10,274. Loans granted by the C.M.H.C.

amounted to 8,149 in Quebec to 9,653 in Ontario, that is a difference of about 500 additional loans granted to Ontario. But this is not the point.
The amount of those loans was $148,619,000 for Quebec compared with $301,725,000 for Ontario.
Mr. Speaker, I do not object, because loans amounting to $300 million have been granted to Ontario. However, I object, because it is so difficult in Quebec to have loans approved by the C.M.H.C.
When assessments are asked, not much enthusiasm is shown. When a large loan is asked in Quebec, there is a certain hesitation, while in Ontario the amount of the loans are twice higher than in Quebec.
I am therefore drawing the attention of the minister responsible for the C.M.H.C. on that situation, so that the officials may be advised to be slightly more tolerant and speedy when loans of the corporation are to be granted in the province of Quebec. I do not ask that Quebecers be favoured to the detriment of others, but that they be treated on the same footing as the people of other provinces, especially Ontario.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I should now like to talk about the part of the budget dealing with social development.
Nowadays, when the government invents a new tax, it does not call it a federal tax, but a social development tax. It sounds better. People complain a bit at first, but they soon become accustomed to it.
That is what I tried to illustrate when I told the house one day about the reactions of a frog. When a frog is thrown into a pail of boiling water, it cannot stand the heat and tries to jump out. You have to be canny and put the frog in a pail of cold water, then slowly allow the water to come to the boiling point. The frog, by that time, is so used to the temperature that it is completely cooked and does not even have time to think of jumping out of the boiling water. The same goes for the Canadian people.
I have here, Mr. Speaker, a letter from a labourer living in Drummondville. Any labourer could have written the same thing and there are many more across the country who share the same opinion. This letter is addressed to the right honourable Prime Minister, Parliament of Canada, Ottawa and it is dated October 25, 1968. This man is not afraid to sign his name: A. Lafontaine, 570,
The Budget-Mr. Caouette 105th avenue, Drummondville. This is in the constituency of the hon. Minister of Industry and Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin). I quote.
I am writing about this new so-called "social development" 2 per cent tax. I was deeply interested in your election campaign and I had thought that a newly elected government would endeavour to straighten out the injustices that have prevailed for a number of years in the income tax system.
I am referring in particular to the income tax rates affecting those families with dependants, where there is only one wage-earner. At present, my monthly salary is $440 and I have been an employee of the Canadian Pacific for 20 years. Nevertheless, sometime within the next three months, I will have to move to another locality that is unknown to me at the present time, because of technological changes by the Canadian Pacific (CSC) with the approval of the Transport Commission-
I do not know where he is moving.
This amounts to saying that this year, besides disruption in my work, your government is putting another 2 per cent increase in my income tax, which means I will have to pay $44 more. It would appear that in my case and that of others-
Every working man.
-we are a cause of inflation in the country. Did you or your Mr. Benson ever figure out the minimum of money required to raise and educate three growing children? And how about the money left over at the end of the year after earning an inflationary monthly salary of $440? The answer to this is that for some years my savings amount to a large ZERO even with driving to work in a 1959 Volkswagen.
Can you explain how the so-called experts in your government arrive at the conclusion that I am a cause of inflation across the country, as I can hardly make ends meet, and that a limit of $120 should be established on all earnings, whatever may be the amount, in the case of the additional 2 per cent tax.
Mr. Prime Minister, is this your "just society" and is it in agreement with the Carter commission report?
Mr. Trudeau, I would like you to refer to Le Devoir of October 23, 1968, on page 15, where it is reported that Imperial Oil has realized net profits of $70 million over nine months.
Kindly let me know what surtax those corporations will have to pay. And why I am, at $440 per month, a cause of inflation in this country, and why should I pay a surtax?
Thanks for having read me.
I do not know whether the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has read this letter, but I read it to the house to make sure that people would know. All Quebec workers could write the same thing.
During the election campaign, the right hon. Prime Minister said nothing about increasing the taxes of Canadians. No minister ever mentioned that taxes would be

Mr. Speaker, social development means, first of all, that an attempt will be made to decrease, or avoid, or eliminate the estimated deficit of $675 million, and here I should like to point out to the house that the interest on the national debt, for this year only, will cost $1.5 billion, that means $75 per citizen. That means that a family of five, husband and wife and three children, will pay $375 in interest on the national debt.
That is why we ask the government to change not only its tax policy, but the fundamental policy, the financial policy.
The financial system is wrong. It is a system of indebtedness and this year, the government carved into the interest on the debt. Do you know that if we did not have to pay that interest, there would be a surplus of almost $1 billion, instead of a deficit of $675 million? When we suggest that the government use the services of the Bank of Canada to finance the development of our natural resources, when we suggest that on the national, provincial, municipal and school levels, everything be financed through the Bank of Canada, without interest, for periods of time varying according to the things that are being created or build, there are some who fear inflation.
Mr. Speaker, has anyone ever heard a Liberal or a Conservative member say, when the government goes to the United States to borrow $500 or $700 million that this is not Canadian money but American credit? It is not a question of American dollars or printed bills being sent to Canada. No. These are cheques sent to us by Americans, new figures entering Canada. In exchange, we have contracted obligations or undertaken to reimburse capital and interest after a certain time.
Did you ever consider that those amounts coming from the United States represent money newly created and as such responsible for inflation? No. We do not hear a single economist on the government side referring to inflation on that occasion. Neither do we hear a single economist on the opposition side referring to inflation when we are contracting debts in the United States. However, as soon as someone suggests resorting to the services of the Bank of Canada, at once inflation is mentioned. If the Bank of Canada should make available the same amount of credit, this would be inflation. When credit is made

available in Canada, we speak of inflation, but it is not when we get it in the United States in order to bring it into Canada. The Bank may make loans or advances for periods not exceeding six months to chartered banks, or to banks to which the Quebec Savings Bank Act applies, on the pledge or hypothecation of certain classes of securities.

Why did the government not suggest to amend this paragraph of the Bank of Canada Act by deleting the words "six months" so that the Bank of Canada could grant advances and loans to provinces, municipalities, school boards, to set up a branch of the Bank of Canada in each of the Canadian provinces, formally instructed to grant the necessary credit for the development of these provinces, municipalities and school boards. That is why-the Minister of Finance was made aware of this fact a few days ago-the provinces are dissatisfied with the central government. It is because of the monetary question, not the fiscal question. The taxation of the Minister of Finance is the crowning achievement of the tax system which is ours.
