speechtext:
I sincerely hope, Mr. Speaker, that this speech has been worth waiting for because there seems to be a great deal of difficulty in proceeding with it. Apparently there are a few traditions here which I should follow, I suppose, one of which seems to have fallen into disuse. I refer to the practice of congratulating Your Honour on your elevation to your high office. I should like to join in those felicitations. Another tradition seems to be that of saying a few words in French. Unfortunately my mastery of that language is rather limited to "l'addition s'il vous plait" and such other
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Bechard).]
DEBATES	November 7, 1968
phrases as permit me to get by in the restaurants of Montreal. I can only say that I shall count myself a failure if four years from now I cannot do better.
It is also, customary, I believe, on the occasion of one's maiden speech to eulogize one's riding, particularly if there is some hope of the home press printing the remarks verbatim and with approbation. Fortunately for all present, I can forgo that pleasant exercise since nothing I could say here, even though I were speaking from the treasury benches rather than this lofty perch, could significantly enhance the existing renown of the city of Calgary. We have our majestic mountains to the west, our rolling foothills and our prolific grain fields which cause so much heartburn to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin). We also have clear running water or had, at least, until pollution. There is one aspect of our life which is unique and bears comment. I refer to the meteorological phenomenon known as the Chinook. This is an unseasonably hot west wind. Its visitations have been associated by the unscientific with sittings of the British Columbia legislature.
I feel I must also take this opportunity to set the record straight with regard to the speech in this house on October 24 by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Wool-liams). I must hasten to assure the house that I am not deliberately associating the hon. member and the unseasonably hot west winds. The proximity of the two subjects is purely coincidental. The comment, "You already have the facts", attributed to me at page 2016 of Hansard, and which was taken by the hon. member for Calgary North to have been made by me was, in fact, made by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) who sits immediately in front of me. I had considered asking that the record be corrected, but listening to the balance of the hon. member's speech made me realize that such correction would, in the eyes of posterity at least, destroy much of the cogency, pertinence and indeed beauty of his oratorical pyrotechnics. Since much of what is said by hon. members opposite is evidently for posterity, as it relates but little to the present, I decided, with characteristic charity, not to ask for a correction. I do hope, though, that future generations perusing the Hansard volumes in whose authorship we are all at present collaborating will not be so emotionally drained by the eloquence of the hon. member that all else seems anti-climatic and this correction is never noted.
November 7, 1968
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Canada's petroleum industry, based in Calgary, is of vital importance to out country measured by any standard. It is at present subject to a number of very serious pressures which are giving rise to grave and legitimate concern in the industry.
One of the parameters relative to which the industry has operated since 1960 has been the national oil policy-a voluntary policy agreed to by the industry and sanctified by government. The basic provision is that petroleum products marketed west of the Ottawa river shall be manufactured from domestic crude oil, while products marketed east of the Ottawa river may be manufactured from imported crude oil. It is a voluntary policy enforced by persuasion by the National Energy Board. The board has no sanctions available if it is breached.
One of the pressures on the policy has been the recent expansion of refinery facilities east of the Ottawa at a rate far in excess of market requirements, coupled with a practical hiatus in refinery expansion west of the Ottawa. A second pressure has been the request of the United States oil administrators, disclosed on September 28, that United States importers of Canadian crude cut back their purchases during the last quarter of this year. There is apprehension that this cut-back may be extended into 1969.
A third pressure is the implication of the Prudhoe bay strike in Alaska. Bearing in mind recent policies enforced by the Securities and Exchange Commission in the United States relative to public companies, for example, the Texas Gulf Sulphur and Douglas Aircraft cases, it is probable that the extent of the Alaska discovery has been understated by the companies concerned. Nevertheless, the announcement indicates a discovery which could well be larger than east Texas, now the biggest field on this continent, and larger than present total reserves of all the known oil fields in Canada, excepting only the Athabasca tar sands.
The concern of our petroleum industry is real and it is well founded. It is, therefore, gratifying to note that clause 15 of the income tax resolution will assist significantly in eliminating the unfair competition implicit in certain prospective artificial crown corporation arrangements between provincial authorities and promoters. Clauses 13 and 14 will also be welcomed by everyone with a bona fide concern about the well-being of
The Budget-Mr. Mahoney Canada, the Canadian petroleum industry, and the people employed in it.
The Alaska discovery gives rise to another matter which I would urge the government to regard as top priority. It is only a matter of hours, days, perhaps months but certainly not years, until a major oil strike will occur in the Canadian Arctic. The Canadian government will find itself, overnight, in the oil business in a very big way. By the very nature of the business initial decisions and policies will have very long range effects. It is imperative that they be right. Let us formulate these policies now. Let us formulate them in consultation with every element of the industry and not merely in consultation with the public service. The right hon. Prime Minister is on record as wanting to recruit talent from business and other environments for special assignments in government. This is an opportunity; indeed, I might suggest, a necessity.
A third consequence of the Prudhoe bay discovery is the necessity of transporting this oil to its markets in the United States. An all-United States routing would probably traverse by pipeline the Brooks range, which separates the north slope from the rest of Alaska, to the vicinity of Anchorage and then involve shipment by tanker to various ports on the Pacific Coast. In addition to extremely difficult construction problems through the Brooks range, this route offers serious seasonal shipping hazards in the north Pacific and a rather obvious strategic exposure. A more desirable all-pipeline route may be found along the Arctic shore to the Mackenzie delta and then south to connect with existing Canadian systems. The strategic and climatic problems would be eliminated by such a routing.
I would urge that the government actively press for the second routing; it is most desirable from the United States point of view and they should be prepared to pay a fair price for it, including elimination of present duties on Canadian crude oil, establishment of fair prorations of the Canadian and Alaskan crude to be transported through such system and a substantial Canadian share in its ownership.
Speaking in this debate a few days ago then hon. member for Etobicoke (Mr. Gillespie) read the following words from the study commissioned by the Toronto Stock Exchange on the supply of, and demand for, Canadian equities:
The total average annual demand for additional equities in Canada in the immediate years ahead is likely to be almost double the supply provided through net new Canadian issues.

2534	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Mahoney
It has been proven in the case of Alberta Gas Trunk Line Company Limited, Great Canadian Oil Sands Company Limited and companies of this nature that Canadian investors wish to participate in the establishment of a Canadian route, I urge the government to give our investors an opportunity to participate.
From Canada's own point of view, the first alternative, the trans-Alaska line coupled with tanker shipment, does nothing to prepare for the marketing of our own anticipated Arctic production. The Arctic Coast-Maeken-zie river route would provide a basic part of the system we will need some day soon in any case.
The rejection in the budget speech of the basic premise of the Carter report that "a buck is a buck is a buck" must be greeted with relief by all thinking Canadians. While acknowledging the desirability of further, even extensive, tax reforms we cannot afford the luxury of a tax system which, however appealing to the theorist, is totally incompatible with those of our trading partners in the free world.
As long as Canada finds it desirable to develop its resources and productive capacity at a rate faster than its own savings permit- and this is a situation likely to exist for the foreseeable future-Canada must maintain fiscal policies calculated to attract foreign investment. If we are to reduce the need for foreign investment in the foreseeable future while still providing a standard of living acceptable to Canadians we must maintain fiscal policies calculated to encourage the formation of investment capital within Canada. Carter ignored these realities; the budget accepts them.
The Company of Young Canadians is a controversial creation of parliament. It is probably the target of as many brickbats from editorial writers and provincial premiers as any federal agency. Yet it is a noble and, I submit, successful experiment. The Company of Young Canadians was created not to supplant existing social agencies but rather to catalyse social change. It is precisely for its success that it is criticized.
The community of Faust on Lesser Slave lake in northern Alberta is populated mainly by Metis, Indians, and white mink ranchers. There are five homes in the community with running water-the rectory, the school principal's home and three homes owned by mink ranchers. Various public agencies working in

DEBATES	November 7, 1968
the community were at odds. For example, the school nurse and the public health nurse were engaged in a jurisdictional dispute over who was responsible for delousing the children. School children were missing as much as 20 per cent of their class time because they were lousy.
Volunteers of the Company of Young Canadians moved in among them and taught them to use the democratic processes available to them-taught them, in fact, that those democratic processes existed. The mink ranchers were furious. They called for withdrawal of the Company of Young Canadians. The full provincial	cabinet met with
representatives of the Metis and Indians. The Company of Young Canadians did not withdraw and there are now seven volunteers working in a number of communities on the lake. Today these people are benefiting from programs under ARDA and two provincial agencies, the human resources development commission and department of youth. There are still only five houses with running water, but the Indians and Metis see hope for change, and the louse count is down. All this was accomplished without disorder or riot, the frustration gap was bridged by the C.Y.C. and the Indians and Metis of the Lesser Slave Lake area are progressing via the democratic process.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
The self-assertion of the Indians at Armstrong, Ontario, is another conspicuous success of the C.Y.C. Never mind the embarrassment occasioned to this government, the Ontario government, the Armstrong school board, or any other authority. These are irrelevant considerations. Think rather of what the Armstrong Indians are accomplishing for themselves. That is the test. The day the C.Y.C. stops embarrassing public authorities and stops jolting the status quo will be the day it will have exhausted its usefulness.
In my own riding there is a district known as Victoria Park. A C.Y.C. volunteer, Bernie Muzeen, worked for two years in the south half of this area. The results of his efforts and, more important, the attitudes which were cultivated among the residents, are a dramatic tribute to the work of the C.Y.C. Crossing 12th Avenue is, in some ways, like passing through Checkpoint Charlie. In the north part of the district blinds are down, the residents withdrawn and apathetic. In the south they are articulate and confident, ready to take on city hall. They will have a brief for
November 7, 1968

the housing task force and any other instrument of authority which presents itself. Their community leaders are among the most effective in Calgary.
The C.Y.C. is to operate on a budget of $1.9 million, some 25 per cent less than its first budget. There are 16 people in its head office and 17 field supervisors. One hundred and eighty-five volunteers in seven of the ten provinces are engaged in 34 projects. These volunteers are living with the negroes of Halifax and the Indians on the tip of Vancouver Island, as well as the hippies of Yorkville.
These young people are fulfilling a vital function in our society-the function of bridging the gap existing between the mainstream of our society and some of its alienated elements. They are doing it for the munificent remuneration of $185 per month, found. And notwithstanding that meagre reward, applications are coming in from young people anxious to serve, at the rate of five a day. There are at present over 500 approved applications for service on file, but they cannot be activated because the company's budget will not permit expansion of its services.
The function of the C.Y.C. is to hook people up with society's mainstream, to show them that a useful democratic process exists and how to use it and then leave them alone to use it themselves. The measure of its success in a given project is the amount of ongoing community leadership it leaves behind. It is, within the limits we have permitted, attacking with success the same festering problem, the alienation gap, as is exploding into riot, pillage and tragedy in other parts of the free world. The government should give serious consideration to whether simply from a dollar and cents point of view the C.Y.C. should not, in fact, be more generously supported. It may very well find that a dime spent on preventive maintenance will save a dollar in repairs.
We are engaged in our regular quadrennial self-reproach at our lack of athletic prowess in international competition. We are also awaiting the report of a task force on amateur sport. We have again underwhelmed the world at the Olympics, trailing not only the obvious giants of international competition such as Russia and the U.S. but some of the less obvious such as Bulgaria and Kenya.
We are, as a nation, at the point where we must decide whether or not we really care. As a matter of fact, we have been at that point for several decades, and we have known it. As another matter of fact, it may
The Budget-Mr. Mahoney not much matter whether we make the decision. Perhaps the exercise of self-reproach and embarrassment on a periodic basis is something to be preserved as character-building and in consequence we should continue to avoid the issue.
We do have some bona fide problems which many other nations do not share. For example, the climate in most parts of the country simply does not permit year-round training in many sports, particularly the track and field events which comprise such an important part of the summer Olympics program. This is not an insoluble problem. Many of the most outstanding American track and field performers come from the northern states. But, of course, they have fieldhouses- large, simple, hangar-like structures-usually with dirt floors where most outdoor activities can be continued in bad weather.
Today there are more than 60 universities and colleges in Canada. Only one, the University of Alberta at Edmonton, has a field-house. That university also has the only full faculty of physical education in Canada. It may be a pure coincidence that the University of Alberta is currently national intercollegiate champion in both hockey and football. It may also be a pure coincidence that the University of Alberta is an institution very little troubled with student unrest. Then, again, it may not be.
Another problem is the very subsidiary position in which competitive sports are generally placed in our public school systems. I am prepared to admit that there may be conspicuous exceptions to this generalization, but it is largely true.
No program which starts working with athletes in their late teens will produce any significant number of medal winners. Such a program is bound to fail unless it is founded on a broad participation in competitive athletics at the elementary school level. Considering the other demands on our educational systems it is appropriate to inquire: what relative priority do we give athletics in terms not only of dollars but of time? From the point of view of national prestige, it should unquestionably be given a high priority. So the question really becomes: what priority should be given by Canadians to measures which will give each of us individually, and the nation as a whole, great pride and satisfaction?
One of the primary objectives of the Olympic movement is to substitute competition on
2536	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Mahoney the playing fields for competition on the battlefield. It is an objective in which we can readily concur. But can we expect the concurrence of persons immediately affected in the proposition that athletic facilities and participation be given a priority ranking with student parking facilities and participation in a good healthy riot?
I am tremendously impressed by the public statements recently made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) on the reorientation of programs within the purview of his department. A brief passage from his speech on October 24 to the national seminar on the planning and construction of health sciences centres merits repetition:
This is the value basic to our way of life, that society exists to foster the growth of the individual person.
This is the end to which our policies must be directed. This is the objective which the C.Y.C. is helping to achieve in many areas. It is the end which achievement in international athletic competition would serve. It is also an objective which is becoming harder to achieve ini an increasingly urban environment.
Calgarians share, sometimes to a greater and sometimes to a lesser extent, the problems of all the great cities of this country, this continent and, indeed, this planet. After all, while it is estimated that Calgary's population will reach a million by the turn of the century, Bombay's will reach 30 million. We share the good and the bad. New buildings are going up at a record rate, and so are traffic fatalities. The population which was responsible for the country's greatest relative participation in "Miles for Millions"-34,118 took part last Sunday and over $400,000 was earned-also contains the sick minds which on Hallowe'en hand out apples with razor blades inside, and licorice sticks with needles concealed in them. We also share much of the self-delusion to be found among Canadians. For instance, we have a beautiful neon sign over our airport which proclaims it as an international airport. But it is not an international airport at all.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
The fourth annual review of the Economic Council of Canada, published just over a year ago, points up forcefully the inevitable trend to urbanization. It would not be useful to recite the report's conclusions. They boil down to increasing urban affluence, increasing urban population. It would be tragic not

DEBATES	November 7, 1968
to recognize the report's implications. Within a generation four out of every five Canadians will live in a major city. This knowledge establishes the terms of reference within which all our major domestic problems, economic, social and constitutional, must be solved.
Within the next generation our cities will have to be rebuilt almost completely, twice as big and, I hope, twice as good. Within the next generation we will have to build and find the money for more new homes, business buildings and other urban facilities than we have built and paid for since Jacques Cartier set foot in Canada.
One of the greatest handicaps to the possibility of our successfully meeting this challenge is the very simple truth that we are on our own. We have no precedents because, unfortunately, no one alive today has ever experienced a really good city, a city that comes even close to measuring up to the potential of today's technology, a city, for example, whose busy streets are not clogged with parked and moving cars, whose air is fit to breathe, and whose water is fit to swim in.
The malaise of our cities could be cured a lot faster if the public could be given a better understanding, a clearer vision, of what kind of city to demand. We must close the communications gap between the planners whose eyes are fixed on the future and the public whose understanding is fixed in the past. What we need and what the government can give is a fresh vision of what tomorrow's city and tomorrow's city living can and should be. The announcement yesterday by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) of the establishment of an urban transportation and development unit in his department is an example of the things that can be done at this level to encourage this vision.
The challenge is not merely one of getting a necessary job done. By the end of the century our large city population will have doubled. Hence, one way or another we are going to have to build new cities and rebuild old ones. The real challenge is not whether but how we build. We may build well or we may build carelessly, but one way or another we will build.
I do not subscribe to the theory that Canada can solve all the world's problems. I do suggest that we can solve our own problems in a way that will serve as a worth-while example to the world.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since coming to parliament I have
November 7, 1968

been engaged in numerous discussions concerning welfare problems. Like all members I have become involved in the problems of my constituents relating to inadequate, unjust, or seemingly unjust, treatment of welfare recipients. At the same time I have become increasingly aware of the enormous economic pressures on this and other levels of government, much of it due to the proliferation of welfare programs. Many, if not most, of these are good and necessary. Most were implemented to meet genuine needs. Some were simply election bait or sops to pressure groups. Many were well intentioned and well designed for their particular purpose and time. Times, however, have changed. The welfare needs of today are not the needs of a decade or more ago.
Our problems today are largely problems of affluence. We have developed a society where the luxuries of yesterday are the necessities of today. At the same time we are saddled with programs which provide services to those who do not require them, while at the same time inadequately serving those who need them desperately. And we are doing this voluntarily, at enormous cost and with tragic inefficiency. The bills are coming in for payment and the overdraft can be crippling- crippling to the taxpayer, crippling to the economy, and crippling to those in genuine need, particularly the physically handicapped and the aged, the aged without resources and those on fixed incomes. We cannot and dare not let this situation continue. It is both stupid and inhumane.
In seeking alternatives I cannot help but be attracted by what I choose to call a guaranteed incentive income. My initial instincts, Mr. Speaker, oppose a guaranteed annual wage. I have not found that things come easily in life and I believe it unrealistic to expect something for nothing. I consider it downright immoral to expect those willing to work to support those who will not.
On the other hand we do have an obligation to those who, for quite legitimate reasons, cannot support themselves. Because we, as Canadians, accept our obligations to this latter group we have built up a system of social welfare that is wasteful, inefficient, inconsistent, discourages initiative and is often demeaning. We have an ever-expanding bureaucracy and we end up, in many cases, paying money to those who do not need it, while frequently not adequately helping those who do.
The Budget-Mr. Danson
It is apparent to me that our entire welfare system needs close examination and revision. In this process we should explore every approach, including the negative income tax which in effect is what some call a guaranteed minimum income or guaranteed annual wage. Properly structured it can save the taxpayers tens of millions of dollars. One recent estimate indicated the amount would be $200 million yearly in Canada today. This does not include the vast savings in administrative costs and the massive reduction in our bureaucracy.
At this juncture I should like to say that I am not criticizing the civil servants who form the bureaucracy, but the expanding bureaucracy itself. Since coming here I have gained a renewed respect for our public servants. There is a wealth of talented and dedicated men and women who do this nation proud and, incidentally, keep it operating on an ethical level unsurpassed anywhere. I am impressed and we should be grateful even if at times they speak in a jargon that is forcing many of the uninitiated to become trilingual rather than simply seeking the enrichment of bilingualism. Certainly there are exceptions, and the vast majority of skilled and devoted civil servants are the first to spot and acknowledge them, but the same applies to any big business and, unlikely as it may seem, to politicians. The same applies also to welfare recipients.
To get back to my basic theme, Mr. Speaker, I believe we should determine what income is necessary to provide the fundamental necessities of food, clothing and shelter. To this we should add the cost of health insurance and education, and enough discretionary money to maintain one's dignity. This would have to be scaled according to the size of the family unit.
Let us for now assume that for a married couple with two school age children this worked ut to $3,000 yearly or roughly $60 per week-hardly a princely sum. With an income of $3,000 they would not pay income tax. As the family produced additional income they would pay income tax on a graduated scale so that they would have the incentive to work and better their lot. This tax would therefore have to be quite small on the initial income increases. Should their income fall below $3,000 they would receive payments to make it up.
Certainly there will always be those who would be satisfied to live on the minimum
2538	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Danson income, just as there are those who are content to live off our existing welfare programs. These people are not unemployed but are kept busy running from office to office filling out forms in quadruplicate. The difference is that much of our present welfare discourages those who want to work and are capable of supplementing their income. In many cases it encourages people to lie and cheat, and requires a large force of civil servants to administer and police it.
With the negative income tax combined with the guaranteed base we could eliminate all or most of our existing systems-unemployment insurance, family allowances, old age pensions, mothers' allowances, rent subsidies and a myriad of other benefits available from federal, provincial, municipal and some private agencies. We would in effect eliminate the means test while actually making need the only criterion.
Of necessity this is an oversimplified version of the scheme. We would have to utilize our existing computer technology to react quickly to immediate needs. A man suddenly out of work cannot wait until tax time to get the money to feed and clothe his family. This might be done by interim loans repayable at tax time if his yearly income exceeds the base. This might be done also through special arrangements with our banks, with the government guaranteeing the loans. The base itself, and the tax on the income above it, would have to be sensitively gauged.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
There is the further question of regional disparities in living costs, but under present federal schemes payments are equal in all parts of the country, as are federal taxes. Rather than present a problem, this scheme could solve many. Currently welfare recipients are inclined to relocate in the provinces or municipalities with the most generous welfare schemes, placing an undue burden on those jurisdictions and their taxpayers. If these people remained in their own localities they would create consumer markets in depressed areas which would then require business and industry to service them. This plan could help solve part of our problems in regional development and prevent the uprooting of family units.
With these potential advantages we should not reject the minimum income principle out of hand, while still exploring all other avenues. It could be the greatest true social and economic reform in our country's history. It

DEBATES	November 7, 1968
could give greater equality, opportunity, prosperity and dignity, while at the same time saving taxpayers untold millions of dollars. In my view this might well be the ultimate rationalization of our present outdated welfare programs and it should be acceptable to the whole range of our political spectrum, as well as all levels of government.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I had intended to give a serious discourse on the report of the task force on the structure of Canadian industry, commonly known as the Watkins report. The subject is a serious one but it also is detailed and I have decided not to bore you or other hon. members with it at this time, not because it is unimportant-on the contrary, it is extremely important-but because I shall save it for another occasion, probably before the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs. I put it aside at this time because of a 15J year old girl named Deb Shallhorn from Markham, Ontario. Deb wrote to me because I am her member of parliament, not her father's member of parliament, not her mother's nor her neighbour's, but hers. She makes me proud to be so.
Deb had heard about the speech by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) in Montreal a week ago Monday in which he suggested the concept of a non-military draft as a way in which our youth can truly be part of this country and its future. This year she is going on a student exchange to Quebec, and that is great; but Deb is doing that for herself and I commend her for it. She also wants to do things for other people and for her country. Are we to deny her that opportunity? Deb's letter is typical of many letters I received prior to the Secretary of State's speech and reflects the response I have seen in the letters to the editor columns of newspapers across this country. It reflects the aspirations which were apparent by the participation of our youth in the June election-happy, enthusiastic, a little mad, but stimulating to us all.
If we dampen that spirit, that idealism, that outrageous and at the same time delightful naivety, we will be doing a tragic disservice to all the Deb Shallhorns and their brothers across this land. If we overconcern ourselves with our problems and neglect them, if we neglect to look into their hearts and minds and fail to see the beauty and the truths that are their hopes, we will see their disillusionment, and even bitterness, that will not be without justification.
November 7, 1968	COMMONS
You might ask what this has to do with the budget. In my opinion it has a good deal to do with the budget because it will cost us money, not in expenditure but in investment. If we are able to achieve the basic welfare structure I have just outlined or, perhaps better, if we can determine our true national needs and national goals, the real ones, the ones that really count, we can go ahead with a spirit and purpose that befit this great nation, a nation we all love deeply and a nation which offers opportunities that make most of the world respectfully envious.
We sometimes become so preoccupied with our problems that we fail to see what we really have going for us. Certainly we have problems which we must attack immediately, intelligently and vigorously. But we will not solve them all, and when some are solved there will be new ones we never suspected, with or without computers, which would appear. But that is the way life is and it is not going to change. Without making light of these problems, let us also look at the bright side because it is just as real as the dark side, and much more hopeful.
I suspect, and my mail tends to confirm this, that is it not really taxes people are complaining about, but rather stupid taxing methods and stupid expenditures. If we tell people we intend to balance budgets and do not, or do not honestly explain the errors which we make because we happen to be human, they will not trust us. If we were to tell people that we intend to spend less, provide more services and lower taxes, we would be bigger fools than the few gullible people who would believe us.
On the other hand, if we do those things that, to a reasonable degree, fulfill the needs of our people and do those things that help fulfil the potential of this land and of the Canadian people, I am confident that the people will go along or, perhaps more accurately, join with us and pay their share, if not happily at least with understanding and even satisfaction. We should not do things to excite; we should do exciting things. We need not capture the imagination of others but should use our imagination to do imaginative things. If we do not do this, then we will be away behind the vast majority of Canadians, and light years behind our youth with whom we will never be able to communicate.
I should like to offer a challenge. It is a challenge to all the Deb Shallhorns across Canada. I want them to talk to their parents about a year's service to their country, or
DEBATES	2539
The Budget-Mr. Moores perhaps a series of three or four summers' service, not necessarily on a compulsory basis but even on a voluntary basis. It need not necessarily be on a non-military basis either, because I would think there might even be many young men who would want to spend part of their service in our armed services so that they could get some insight into the possibility of serving in what is our likely role, that of a peacekeeping nation, or perhaps in our coastguard or the R.C.M.P., all very challenging careers. I suggest that they talk to their parents and then write to me indicating that they have their parents' approval even though they know it will cost them more in taxes. I challenge their parents to explain what this means in cost and perhaps encourage their children to take paper routes, become baby sitters, or engage in any other job that will produce money which they must save in order to help their parents pay these extra taxes, because with opportunity goes responsibility. If they respond responsibly we will find ways to make certain that they will indeed have the opportunity, including the opportunity to have all the education they can absorb.
I tell these youth that if they do these things and if they and their parents write to me, I will go to the Secretary of State and to my Prime Minister and fight for these things on their behalf. I am sure I will receive a sympathetic response. But that is not the end of my challenge. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I challenge all hon. members of this house to react to the challenge of our times, to the challenge of our youth whom we are here to serve. We do not dare let them down. I do not mean by that that we will fulfil all their dreams, but they will know we are working in their interest and that of our country's future. We must not look only at the difficulties because that route would stop us cold. We must not be afraid of failure, for there is no disgrace in failure. The disgrace is in not trying.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that in a member's initial speech to this house it is customary to take his fellow members on somewhat of a tour of his constituency. I do not intend to do this because the constituency of Bonavista-Trinity-Conception was represented in this house for some 20 years by well known Liberal members. While I am sure they eulogized on many occasions the rugged beauty of Bonavista-Trinity-Conception, at
2540	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Moores the same time they were leading its people up the garden path.
After listening to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) outline the terms of his budget many people in Newfoundland must have questioned whether Ottawa has really ever admitted that our province was taken into the Canadian federation in 1949. Certainly the philosophy and policies of this government as revealed so starkly in this budget give no indication of any concern for the special problems of Newfoundland or any intention to do anything to solve them.
Like Canadians in every part of our country, Newfoundlanders are being squeezed to the brink and in many cases over the brink of poverty by the pincers of taxation and inflation. It has been estimated that almost 40 per cent of the people of Newfoundland receive some government aid in some form. On this basis it may be argued that not too many people in my province will be affected by a tax increase for the simple reason that most of them do not make enough income to be taxed. But even those who are on direct relief will experience the pinch exerted by the Minister of Finance here in Ottawa. His budgetary measures will affect the lives and prospects of every Canadian whether he pays direct taxes or not.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The trouble is that everything is multiplied in shock effect in Newfoundland. The economy is more basic than in any other province; the wages are lower, the opportunities fewer and prices higher. Living is tough in Newfoundland and getting tougher. This budget is just one more blow below the belt. One of the shortest and best descriptions of it that I have read appeared in that staunch Liberal mouthpiece, the Winnipeg Free Press. On October 23 an editorial appeared headed simply "Dismal". Naturally it was a comment on the Minister's budget. I quote in part:
Finance Minister Benson's budget is a confession of grievous financial miscalculation on the part of the federal government, coupled with a pious promise to do better next year. There is in it little cause for cheer.
Later it goes on to say:
It is beyond comprehension how Mr. Benson can in one breath be warning people that his government intends to increase its spending by more than $1 billion, and in another be expressing anxiety about the continuation of an inflationary upward spiral of prices and costs. A substantial factor in present inflationary pressures is the amount of money being spent by government at all levels.

DEBATES	November 7, 1968
This strikes at the very heart of Atlantic Canada's problem and the current disillusionment of Atlantic Canadians with the present government. This government is squandering money on a wide variety of inconsequential things, money desperately needed by the provinces of Atlantic Canada. One has only to think of the thousands of dollars being poured into the redecoration of ministerial offices and the building up of personal retinues, including that of the Prime Minister. One cannot help but think too of the expensive ministerial junket to South American countries which has just been embarked upon by a considerable segment of the cabinet.
There are many other expensive items such as the millions being sunk in commissions and task forces that could be curtailed and the money used for critical development work in the battle to overcome regional disparity and poverty. This government appears to be able to find ample funds for its own hobbies and enjoyment. The minister pours tax dollars into his colleagues' spending plans as though they came from an inexhaustible cornucopia.
The federal government does not realize that the most important obligation it had and has to its newest and tenth province. Rather than providing the people with opportunities to get ahead, rather than creating a long term plan whereby Newfoundlanders could earn a decent living, it takes the attitude that handouts will suffice.
The federal government has disbursed funds on a basis that could be compared to the well known concept of the American foreign aid program whereby if enough money is given, even at the cost of human decency and self-respect the recipients should still be thankful. A great deal of federal money has come to Newfoundland since 1949. Most of it has been spent at the whim of a fiscally irresponsible provincial leader, completely unused to economic planning. The victims of this irresponsibility have been the people of Newfoundland, who today enjoy the lowest per capita income and the highest cost of living, resulting in the lowest standard of living in Canada.
After 20 years of squandering, the result is only now being fully realized. Since confederation, the premier of Newfoundland should be commended for advances in health, education and social services. However, he should be brought to task for his completely irresponsible fiscal policies. A gentleman who likes to be referred to as the only living father of
November 7, 1968

confederation, with his proven ability to squander money on grandiose deals, to cook up promotions with people of the Doyle, Sha-heen ilk, should not be referred to as the only living father of confederation but rather as the only living "Daddy-O" of confederation.
At the same time as personal ministerial kingdoms are being financed, the Prime Minister tells the provinces bluntly: The till is empty, look after yourselves; you cannot have any of my 2 per cent surtax because it is not really an income tax but a social development tax. I only wish this statement were true. There would then be some hope that the urgent social needs of my province would get support here in Ottawa.
The tragic part of the budgetary policies of this government is that they are seeking to give the impression of economizing, not by cutting down frivolous and unnecessary spending but by cutting out vital and necessary programs of national and regional development. The time has come when the federal government must make positive long term plans whereby the fishery sector of our economy will be developed. When one realizes how important the fish industry is to eastern Canada one must also realize how important this industry could be if properly developed. At the present time fish and fish products represent close to 3 per cent of Canada's gross export value. In Newfoundland at the present time there are approximately 30,000 people involved in the fish industry; together with their dependants they represent some 120,000 people, which in turn represents approximately one-quarter of our population.
This industry today, through neglect and lack of planning, is very near collapse and, Mr. Speaker, this is not an exaggeration. Many fishing companies in Newfoundland have been family affairs, and with the limited resources and fluctuations in managerial ability, which are factors in hereditary businesses, the industry has failed to keep up with international marketing techniques and the technological advances that are so necessary in today's world. To survive, the industry needs federal development funds on the scale provided by European countries to their fisheries.
When one considers that Newfoundland has the nearest proximity to the greatest ground fish resources in the world, it is very upsetting to see the huge government sponsored developments, of European countries in particular, fishing in what are commonly
The Budget-Mr. Moores referred to as Canadian waters while we in Canada are neglecting this industry.
When one realizes that the Canadian deep sea fleet consists of approximately 40,000 tons of shipping while the European fleet fishing in the northwest Atlantic represents in excess of 2,800,000 tons, it makes one stop to think. I will repeat the ratio in a slightly different manner. For every ton of deep sea fishing craft leaving Canada's ports there are approximately 80 tons of deep sea fishing craft from Europe operating off our coast. If all the fish presently caught in the northwest Atlantic were processed in Canada the value would be several times the total contribution of all agricultural products combined.
The fishing industry off the east coast of Canada should be playing a much more prominent part than is the case today. However, if we are going to bridge the disparity which is so prevalent in eastern Canada we must come up with a long term plan for fishery development, together with a short term plan to make sure that there is an industry left when all the task forces and study groups have finally reached their conclusions. I have repeatedly mentioned that the fishing industry has been neglected in Newfoundland. There is danger of it becoming extinct. This must not be allowed to happen.
Yet our government is cutting expenditure, cutting in the wrong places, cutting out a just society rather than creating one. Every member of the government from the Prime Minister down has served notice on the provinces that these are lean years and they should expect nothing but cut-backs. What this means to Atlantic Canada literally, Mr. Speaker, is disaster. This government has made a big thing of regional disparity. They have even set up a new department to administer its affairs. But nowhere, least of all in this budget, is there any sign that the government knows the dimensions of regional disparity or where in fact it exists, let alone that it has any answers to the problem.
Let me say right now that the worst area of regional disparity in the provinces and territories that make up Canada is in the province of Newfoundland. If it were not so pathetic one could laugh at recent statements made by a Newfoundlander, the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Jamieson), speaking last month at Grand Falls. He referred to the 20 years of notorious mistakes on the part of the provincial government as merely "mistakes of the heart". He said that "slide-rule theorists" and "hard-hearted administrators"
2542	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Moores would not raise the standard of living in Newfoundland. I agree with him entirely, but I wonder whether he was thinking of his cabinet colleagues or some of the senior civil servants he ostensibly controls as a minister of the crown.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
He advocated that we "abandon the conventional kind of approach to our problems" and use "a sound head and reasonable approach". With all this I agree wholeheartedly, and the minister undoubtedly would have been listened to closely if he had not made one further statement to the effect that the Prime Minister recognized Newfoundland's problems and endorsed unconventional methods of solving them. This is just too much to swallow. If the Prime Minister felt this way about Newfoundland and her problems, he would never have had placed before us such a despairing and barren document as this budget.
The truth of the matter is that no purposeful, co-ordinated attack has been mounted on Newfoundland's problems. I might suggest to our new government that even though the premier of Newfoundland was so obviously friendly to the right hon. Prime Minister at the Liberal leadership convention, it would be wise for the government of Canada, when making funds available to Newfoundland, to have the terms well thought out, to have well planned economic policies which will have a lasting effect on our people, and not provide funds for merely political reasons to continue the one-man distribution system that has been in vogue for the last 20 years.

What we cannot afford is to see these two spiritually united gentlemen walk over the Newfoundland countryside into the sunset, knee to knee, heart to heart, brain to brain, hand in hand, with God walking a respectful ten paces behind.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Because of its centuries of isolation, its rugged and detached geography and its dependence upon one or two basic

DEBATES	November 7, 1968
resource industries, Newfoundland has been in a special category and has presented a special challenge. Let me stress right here, Mr. Speaker, that solving this problem, meeting this challenge, is not a question of charity to the needy or helping the less fortunate in society. This is a truly national problem and a truly national emergency.
The halfhearted imposition of the 12-mile limit is another example of too little too late. It is now imperative that the government come to the defence of our east coast fishery in a positive and courageous manner, not in the pussyfooting manner in which the Biafran situation was handled but with the firm purpose that is mandatory when a part of the Canadian body is withering away.
Nothing short of taking over the management of our marine resources on the continental shelf, and taking that step now, will save our offshore fishery from going into the decline that the delay in the implementation of the 12-mile limit effected in our inshore fishery. I know all about the delicate international feelings this government is so long-windedly careful not to ruffle; but if Peru can make a unilateral definition of its territorial waters, surely the great nation of Canada can do no less. No nation such as Canada can afford to let any part of its economy atrophy without endangering the whole body. Newfoundland's prosperity is as much in the interest of the other provinces as it is of the people of Newfoundland.
This brings me to the main failure of this budget as seen through the eyes of Newfoundlanders. The federal government has overspent recklessly and thoughtlessly. It now tells the provinces of Canada to cut spending, to live tight. It is high time the federal authorities realized that Canada is composed of regions vastly different in their economic life, moving at varying economic speeds and requiring different and often opposed economic policies.
The old expression, "What is good for General Motors is good for the United States," does not apply to Ottawa and the ten provinces. What may be good at this moment for Newfoundland may not necessarily be what is good for Ontario, for British Columbia or even Ottawa. In a confederation such as ours it is a question of to each his own when we are looking at the disparate regional economies. Today Ottawa is like the spendthrift heir of the Victorian novels who dissipated his inheritance in riotous living. The Atlantic
November 7, 1968

region and, again, Newfoundland in particular, are like the poverty-stricken nineteenth century coal miner trying to get on his feet and find enough food and clothing for his children. Ottawa's plight is not Newfoundland's plight. Ottawa's needs are not Newfoundland's needs. The answers to Ottawa's current problems are quite different from the answers that must be found for those of Newfoundland.
I have said that the basic need of Newfoundland is to bring her economy in balance up to a respectable level. To do this we must start at the bottom. We must provide large scale, long term development of such things as power facilities, highways, resources and education as the foundation for an integrated and co-ordinated economy capable of steady and orderly expansion and capable, too, of providing the standard of living, social amenities and opportunities that are our people's due. We need this foundation upon which to build the secondary and service industries that are so necessary to a well-rounded and healthy regional economy. We need all this to provide the new wealth and the new tax base that alone can ensure that Newfoundland can cease to be a national economic liability and play its rightful role as an equal partner in the community of provinces that is Canada.
To undertake even the preliminary steps in this great enterprise will require federal and provincial government spending on a large scale. It will be necessary at any time, but in times such as these even more so. That is why I say that this budget, the pleas for cut-backs and economy by the Minister of Finance, the whole direction of Liberal policy, are out of step with Newfoundland's and Canada's true needs.
The minister has said the provinces cannot expect any portion of his social development tax revenue. He has said, in effect: the federal till is empty, the federal establishment is near bankruptcy. This is bad for all provinces. It will be a disaster for Newfoundland. The brutal economic fact of Newfoundland life today is that the provincial government is broke too. The provincial debt has almost doubled since 1965. In that year it stood at $502 per capita; today it stands at nearly $1,000 per capita.
Newfoundland cannot do what it must for itself without outside help. The only source for such help is the federal government. But the terms of this budget and the attitude of the minister have given in advance a callous
The Budget-Mr. Moores and unfeeling "no" to any request for financial assistance. The economic crisis in the life of my province has been made more acute by developments in the only two great resource industries already developed to a reasonable degree of productivity, those of fisheries and forestry. Both these basic industries face tougher competition and lower prices in the world market.
The old established inshore fisheries are dwindling both in the number engaged and the revenue taken in. The offshore fisheries have increased in number and volume, but here lower world prices have all but destroyed the advance in productivity. With her few traditional industries in a chaotic state, and new industrial and commercial complexes not yet established, this is a year of desperate prospects for Newfoundlanders.
Last January Mr. Ewart Pratt, president of the Newfoundland board of trade and a member of the advisory board of the institute of social and economic research of Memorial University, stated that Newfoundland needed special incentives and special attention if it was ever to reach economic parity with the rest of the nation. "We all realize that the federal, as well as the provincial government, must exercise a much greater degree of restraint in its spending," he said in the Globe and Mail of January 3. Then he said:
But we do feel that in the Atlantic provinces, and particularly in Newfoundland, we have so far to go to catch up with the rest of Canada that any restraint imposed by the federal government should not apply to us. In Newfoundland we are still well below prevailing economic standards in the other maritime provinces, to say nothing of the wealthier parts of the country.
In times of financial restraint, the emphasis should be on productive projects, enterprises which will benefit the economy of a region and create wealth. To do this, area incentives already exist. But they will have to be further expanded.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Here in a nutshell is our problem. Here in a nutshell is the great failing of this budget. What kind of a business is our Minister of Finance running anyway? In May he forecast a budgetary deficit of $40 million or less. Today the projected deficit stands at an appalling $675 million. I can easily understand the minister being wrong, but what about his army of expert advisers? How long could a man in private business avoid bankruptcy if he ran an operation on that basis? This is the government and this the minister who have the colossal gall to counsel belt tightening and the practice of economy.
2544	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Moores
Estimated federal spending now stands at $10.76 billion or $480 million more than they said they would spend last spring and $190 million more than they thought they would spend as late as last month. If a private concern had a comptroller who was as wide of the mark in his forecasts they would fire him on the spot. The Prime Minister claims he is running a business-like government, and he may take that as some kind of hint or advice.
On October 24 the Montreal Gazette referred to the "grim" budget. This is a mild term to use. The Gazette at that time said:
How serious the situation is may be seen in Mr. Benson's admission that the budget could not be balanced for the current fiscal year, whether the government wished to do so or not. . . This is a grave admission for it amounts to saying that the rate of government spending is now so far out of control that a balanced budget is also out of the government's reach, even supposing that a balanced budget had been its aim.
In other words, this government is floundering out of its economic depth, with no prospect of finding bottom in the next few years.
This is tragic for Canada, and it is doubly tragic for Newfoundland. I can only express the hope that in the months ahead, the time still remaining before federal and provincial governments sit down to discuss shared cost programs, tax apportionment and other similar subjects, the Minister of Finance and his colleagues will give some thought to the special needs of Newfoundland.
I hope this government will recall the pledges made in 1949 at the time of confederation. I hope they will acknowledge the political and moral obligations assumed by Ottawa at that time. I hope they will abandon the makeshift emergency approach to Newfoundland's problem and tackle the question at its roots. It has been mentioned ad nauseam that we are going to have a just society with fair sharing, a society that will look after the regional disparity which Newfoundland, I would think, typifies.
Well, Mr. Speaker, we want a just society. I will support a just society. The one thing I will not support, the one thing I will fight, will be the attitude of the previous administration and this administration of the past three months of a just a little longer society. The people of Atlantic Canada require action and not philosophical platitudes. They want a plan with the objectives clearly defined. They want to make the rest of Canada proud not only of their being fellow Canadians but of their being contributing Canadians.
The popular conception of Newfoundland today is that it is a liability to the rest of

DEBATES	November 7, 1968
Canada. But I would ask the rest of Canada to give Newfoundland and Newfoundlanders the opportunity to be an asset to this great country of which we are all so justly proud.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in the budget debate I take cognizance of the fact that this is my first major address in these very auspicious surroundings. There is, however, one other first related to my rising here this afternoon, and I am very conscious of it. I am very proud to be able to draw it to your attention, Mr. Speaker, and to the attention of this house. This first I refer to is that I have the privilege of being the first Liberal member of parliament to represent Comox-Alberni in this House of Commons.
Although I am the first Liberal member of parliament from my riding, we of Comox-Alberni have been fortunate in having been represented by independent liberals for many years, and at this time I would like to pay tribute to one of those members, the late Mr. A. W. Neill who for many years served his country and his constitutents exceedingly well by his admirable contributions in this house. I hope that my representation on behalf of my constituents will be as effective as Mr. Neill's.
May I now pay tribute and offer my congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) on the contents and presentation of his first budget. His budget is realistic and objective and is directed toward relating the trends of the past to those of the future. Close scrutiny by rational individuals of the budget will result in an appreciation of what the finance minister expects to achieve now and in the year 1969-70. The confidence he exuded in his presentation is reflected in his budget after objective perusal of it by rational individuals.
I am confident that the Canadian people have accepted this budget because they are rational and appreciate the necessity for measures taken in this budget. The public is rational, which is more than can be said for many honourable members on the opposite side of the house, excluding the rump section, of course. The Canadian people realize that services provided by this or any other government must be paid for by the public through one means of taxation or another.
There are those opposite me who would, on the one hand, offer all Canadians a guaranteed annual income, would build a tunnel to Newfoundland, and in brief would create a Utopia for all Canadians, while on the other hand they would decrease the present rate of
November 7, 1968

taxation. These two positions are simply not compatible, and those who take such a stand must surely be classified as irrational and irresponsible, and must have reconciled themselves to accepting the fact that their cries and pleas are going unheard and that they will not be in the position for many, many years to incorporate their absurd, contradictory policies.
As individuals, certainly we begrudge tax increases. I know I do and so do my constituents, but when a government is faced with the necessity of raising substantial additional revenues, as this government is, in order to place its accounts in good order, as Canadians we must endeavour to accept the methods used to raise those revenues.
I must confess I would have preferred, and I know my constituents would have preferred, the 2 per cent social development tax to be graded or graduated with a much higher ceiling so that a much higher proportion of revenues received would have come from individuals in the higher income brackets. As an alternative it may well have been more acceptable, in order to achieve the same purpose, to have had a smaller basic percentage without gradations and limitations.
Tax increase amounts, as well as the amount of taxes we pay, are relative. They are relative to whatever amount is left and to what can be accomplished with the amount that is left. Let me illustrate by reiterating what I as a Canadian taxpayer have often maintained, that under our present tax structure I would have no reluctance in paying $100,000 annual tax because in paying that amount I would be assured of putting a sizeable amount in my pocket. In other words, the amount of tax I pay is of no significance; it is the amount I have left after paying my taxes that is relevant.
I am concerned about the old age pensioner who must pay tax if he has a superannuation supplement because a $20 tax increase related to his net income places him in a much more difficult position than the individual who must pay a $120 tax increase or, if there were no limits on the 2 per cent social development tax, a $240 or a $480 tax increase. I do not sympathize with those who are paying high income taxes nearly as much as I do with those who are paying little or no income tax.
May I now turn to the howling, screaming provincial finance ministers, of whom my own is certainly no exception. These same provincial ministers of finance grope toward Ottawa with long reaching arms seeking
The Budget-Mr. Durante handouts from this government. If I may diverge and draw an analogy for a moment, let me say that they remind me of young pre-school age children at the local fail-reaching out for a grab bag that only costs a pittance but which may contain a prize of inestimable value. These ministers are prepared to take any offering from the federal government, utilize it to their political advantage, pat themselves on the back and, rather than give Ottawa the credit which is due, retaliate by criticizing our fiscal policies.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I should like now to refer to the province of British Columbia and to its finance minister who has gathered together a fleet of ferries of which he is extremely proud, and rightly so. But does he tell the people of his province or the people of Comox-Alberni who must use his ferries in travelling between their homes on Vancouver Island and the mainland of British Columbia, that a good portion of the capital cost of those ferries was paid by this government? I should say he does not. They are his ferries and yet as my colleague, the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour (Mr. Perrault), has repeatedly said, if you were to remove the federal plates from Mr. Bennett's ferries they would sink like stone. Not one would remain afloat.
I do not, however, completely exonerate the federal government from all blame for failing to draw their financial contributions to the provinces to the attention of the Canadian public. A much more thorough job of informing our people of our participation in federal-provincial programs is essential. For example, federal contributions to the province of British Columbia to assist in the construction of the ferries to which I have just referred amounted to $38,486,920.99 from 1961 to 1967. Contributions to technical and vocational training in 1967 to the province of British Columbia amounted to $16,560,000. In the same year, just under $2 million was paid for highways and transportation. Contributions and payments to universities and the National Research Council amounted to $14,450,000 in 1967. I could elaborate further, but suffice to say at this time that the grand total for the year 1967 of federal contributions to British Columbia provincial and municipal governments and of payments to universities, other institutions and individuals amounts to $399,640,000.
From the amounts to which I have referred, Mr. Speaker, I am confident that my
November 7, 1968

The Budget-Mr. Durante constituents in Comox-Alberni received fair consideration, and so they should. May I now take this opportunity to indicate to the house the value of my constituency to the economy of the province in which it is situated and to our country.
Comox-Alberni is an area rich in natural resources. We have lumbering of a nature unprecedented anywhere in our country, commercial fishing with productive fishing grounds on both its west and east coasts, untapped mineral resources in the northern regions, pockets of ideal agricultural land and tourist enticement in every corner. Each of these industries, major in scope, is a vital cog in the Canadian economy and must not be underestimated. As a matter of fact, I accept as my responsibility the importance of keeping this area of our country, Comox-Alberni, well in the minds of our government. In recent years especially there has been a feeling that we in Comox-Alberni have been overlooked by the federal government and its development programs. I serve notice that now and in the future I will expect this government to give special consideration to the development of Comox-Alberni, and other areas of Vancouver Island, and to the development of its resources, including tourism, so that it will progress as rapidly as its potential would indicate.
The development of a west coast national marine park in the Tofino-Ucluelet-Barkley Sound area is a necessity and is to receive my highest priority as well, I hope, as the highest priority of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien). I felt, Your Honour, on hearing that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had taken off for Spain after the election, that he had consulted with his guru and would start immediately, bubbling with enthusiasm, to work out new approaches and new programs which would concentrate on regional development in order to end regional disparities. All that has

really happened is what I told people in my constituency: You will see increases in taxes, you will see unemployment, you will see more cutbacks of construction jobs; but you will not see national policies and programs implemented to counteract our national problems, because the group on the other side is too busy programming this new just age, and listening to McLuhanism. We can no longer neglect young couples who lack housing, nor farmers who have to pay higher interest rates, nor the effect of our postal rates. I say this because people like the friendly publisher and editor of the Edmonton Journal do not forget easily.
As one who has played professional football, I feel the latest budget has to be the greatest squeeze play of all time, as far as the taxpayer is concerned. The latest budget performance is a source of disappointment to Canadians, who were subjected to a 10 per cent tax increase in 1966 and a 3 per cent surcharge in 1968. Now they are faced with a further 2 per cent increase called a social development tax, in addition to the raising of the old age security ceiling to $240, and increased taxes on cigarettes and liquor.
Western Canada, already suffering economically as a result of failure to dispose of a large wheat surplus, will be hurt further by the move to restrict the depletion allowances granted to petroleum and mining companies. It should be remembered that these companies are risking their shareholders' money to bring in new resource development, and that if they are hamstrung by restrictive regulations they will, naturally, be less inclined to take risks. This will mean that a development which benefits every Canadian is slowed down.
Apart from the higher income tax bite, and the restrictions on development, the only new feature in the budget is the inclusion of life insurance companies in the corporation tax area.
Removal of the exemption in connection with medical bills paid by provincial plans exposes the individual taxpayer to a further hike in personal payments. The government has now revealed that medicare could go as high as $370 million. Last year we were promised a balanced budget. Now we are told it will be next year. The budget reveals a seasonal unemployment rate above 5 per cent during the summer months, a mild recession in 1967, with rising inventories and overcapacity in some manufacturing industries, in spite of the stimulating effect of Expo and high tourist spending, which have now largely worn off. Inflation has gone on unchecked.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
Recessive factors have remained in the economy and the government has done little
The Budget-Mr. Paproski to deal with them. We can look forward to growing economic uncertainty and increased unemployment, at least on a regional basis.
The government produced one set of estimates last spring and followed them with a revised set of estimates in the fall, the only difference being an increase of $400 million. It is spending $10.7 billion with revenues of $10 billion, leaving a deficit between income and outgo of nearly $700 million.
If a businessman or corporate manager were to run his business in the same way I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, he would not be in the president's chair for long. The government has engaged in massive commitments through the Canada Pension Plan, the Canada Assistance Plan, and now medicare, while at the same time regrettably falling short in stimulating the expansive and productive sector of the economy at a rate sufficient to support the social welfare expansion.
Let us look at defence. It is interesting to note that defence expenditures have gone up 18 per cent over 1967, and on that ground the economic argument for unification is a complete failure.
The budget fails to cope with high and growing interest rates, high taxes and growing inflation. It does not cope with the problem of increasing real per capita output at a rate to ensure full realization of economic potential. Instead of moving to reduce interest rates, the government created the situation in the first place by removing the ceiling on interest rates. The recent action in amending farm credit and fishermen's credit legislation, to remove the limitation on interest rates, has added to the problem.
In the past two years prices and costs in Canada have risen more rapidly than prices and costs in the United States, in spite of the fact that Canada has not had to contend with the inflationary impact of Viet Nam. There; has been no indication, in the way the government has managed its finances, of a real capacity to manage the economic growth of the nation. We had a 10 per cent tax increase in 1966, an increase in sales and indirect taxes in 1967, and a further 3 per cent surtax on incomes in 1968. In its latest budget the government had to grapple with the problem of closing the $700 million gap between spending and revenues. It had the choice of making a serious attempt to control its spending or come back to the people once again for further revenues. It chose the latter, like the pitcher that went once too often to the well.
November 7, 1968

The Budget-Mr. Mongrain
In his minibudget a year ago the former finance minister promised to keep the increase within a range of 4.5 per cent, or a total of $10.3 billion. This the government did not succeed in doing. A continuing rate of increases in both costs and consumer prices of approximately 4 per cent has added to our economic problems. The Economic Council report describes the increase in real per capita output in 1967 as only about 1 per cent, well below potential.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that the government, although in office only a Short time, already stands indicted by its own record. Canadians are being asked to pay higher and higher taxes to support a record of extravagance unequalled in peacetime history.
Where are the great plans and schemes of the just society? There is nothing in the budget for young Canadians, nothing offering them a challenge, nor is there any outline of the goals and objectives they seek. What of the great frontiers of science, the challenge of the north, the untapped resources of Canada? There is nothing here to challenge the imagination, nothing to inspire, to stimulate or to give hope.
It is evident, Mr. Speaker, that the throne speech, in the uninspired pedestrianism of its prose, was a true reflection of the government's lack of policy, lack of planning and lack of imagination. The budget is an expression of failure; it expresses the government's lack of confidence in itself. It is a vote of non-confidence by the government in its own policies. The government, having so expressed itself, how can this house do less?

Then we found that the provinces had warned the government, whose computerized brains were apparently only capable of ignoring what they learned.
I saw a headline in one of the papers the other day which read: Next Stop The Moon. I thought they were referring to the budget, but apparently it was a reference to the United States space program. These fiscal astronauts opposite, however, are in a class by themselves. I am only wondering what will happen when they try to get back into the earth's atmosphere. I am seriously worried that they will simply burn up, and take the economy with them.
This budget is a confession of the government's abysmal failure to keep expenses in line. On December 6, 1967, I spoke in this

What about the ordinary Canadian?
