speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are three or four areas in the broad field of our financial affairs about which I would like to make some brief comments.
The first area concerns family allowances. When the original legislation pertaining to family allowances was first enacted almost 25 years ago, Canada had very little other social welfare legislation. We did not have old age security, the Canada Assistance Plan, the guaranteed income supplement, provincial hospitalization schemes, the Canada Pension Plan or many other municipal, provincial and federal programs which we now consider basic to the physical and financial well-being of Canadians. It is my submission, Mr. Speaker, that the universal family allowance system as it is now constituted has in some ways outlived its usefulness, and that part of the funds which are now being expended on family allowance could be used more directly and significantly to help certain people in our society to whom we owe a greater measure of assistance. During the fiscal year, 1966-67, we spent more than $600 million on family and youth allowances. If these allowances were not paid for the first child in each family, we would save approximately $250 million each year.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that most families in our present economy can bear the burden of raising their first child without assistance from the government. This figure of $250 million is approximately the same amount as was
DEBATES	2559
The Budget-Mr. Buchanan spent upon the guaranteed income supplement last year. I would suggest that we would be filling a far greater need and discharging a more pressing responsibility to our Canadian citizens if we ceased paying for the first child in each family and instead doubled the guaranteed income supplement. This would mean that all single Canadians who are receiving the old age security pension would be guaranteed a minimum income of approximately $140 per month and that all couples would have a minimum income of $280 per month if they qualified for this supplement. These figures certainly do not provide for luxury living today, but they should much improve the present situation and guarantee our senior citizens a minimum level of dignity in their retirement years.
One nice thing about recommending a program of this type is that it is not a program where we are going to have constantly increasing costs since, over the next eight years, as the Canada and Quebec pension plans come to full maturity the requirement for the guaranteed income supplement may well be eliminated for a large percentage of our retirees.
If this line of thought seems reasonable, Mr. Speaker, and we also discontinued the payment for the second child, when there were only two children in the family, we would realize an additional $75 million. This would mean that in families which had only one or two children there would not be any family allowance paid. But all families which had three children or more would receive payment for all children but the first. Having found the funds, I would like to suggest a method whereby we could now dispose of them.
The fifth annual review of the Economic Council of Canada laid great emphasis on the fact that in Canada's second century the main basis for economic prosperity would be the maximum educational development of our people.
I believe there is one group of young men and young women in our society against whom our government-assisted universities unintentionally discriminate. Maybe this is an unhappy choice of words-I do not mean that they actually discriminate against them but, because of the physical location of our universities, the potential students who live beyond commuting distance from these universities have a far greater financial burden to bear in attending university than do the
November 1. 1968

The Budget-Mr. Buchanan potential students who live in or near university towns or cities. I would like to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we should have some system whereby these potential students who live beyond commuting distance are given a subsistance allowance if they are qualified and wish to attend university. Canada has a total population of approximately 20 million people. Of this figure, roughly 12 million Canadians live within commuting distance of universities. In other words 40 per cent live beyond commuting distance.
Applying these same figures to our present enrolment at universities we find that there would he roughly 100,000 out of a total university population of 250,000 whom we would have to assist. Assuming an average subsistance allowance of $100 per month for the 7J months at university, this would involve a total annual outlay of $75 million.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if we are genuine in our talk about equality of opportunity this is a mandatory step we should be taking to try to make certain that the young men and the young women who live in Goose Bay, or Peace River, or Owen Sound, are put on an equal footing with the students who live in Toronto, Vancouver, Halifax or Edmonton.
The third area on which I would like to make a few comments, Mr. Speaker, concerns the question of shared cost programs. A great deal of concern has been expressed by hon. members opposite about the unbalanced budget which we are going to have this year. I would like to quote from an editorial in last Tuesday's Montreal Gazette:
The disturbing fact is not that the federal government has unbalanced its own budget; it has had its budget unbalanced for it.
The main trouble has come from the shared-cost agreements it made with the provinces in such fields as hospital insurance and post-secondary education. These agreements were not for fixed amounts, such as would have made budgetary prediction possible. They were open-ended, with Ottawa paying a percentage of whatever the provinces spent. This has meant that the federal government has had to meet costs over which it had no direct control. It signed something not unlike blank cheques.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
The whole system of shared cost programs violates a basic concept in a democratic system, which is that the government responsible for spending funds should also be the government responsible for raising these funds. This is how the elected representatives are made accountable to their electors and how, to a large degree, their electors measure their performance. It seems to me, Mr. 

Speaker, that this whole business of shared cost programs flies right in the face of this fundamental democratic principle and I think we should be doing our utmost to eliminate the shared cost programs in which we are presently participating. Mr. Speaker, I realize that this principle cannot operate to its theoretical perfection in a federal system such as ours where we have accepted the idea of striving to achieve equality amongst various regions. Because of this, the federal government must raise funds from the more prosperous regions and give them as grants to the less prosperous regions.
It is also argued that in order to maintain an adequate degree of control over fiscal policies it is necessary for the central government to raise a significant portion of the tax dollars so that the economy can, to some extent, be stimulated or cooled off. However, even if the federal government were to opt out of the shared cost programs, and turn over a certain number of equalized tax points to the provinces, it would still maintain and control approximately 80 per cent of its present tax levying and spending capacity. Therefore I would suggest the basic premise still applies. The government which is spending the money should be the government which is responsible to its electors for raising the money.
Prior to being elected to parliament I was a member of the board of education in my riding. Even there, Mr. Speaker, I discovered that the great concern, understandably, of the elected representatives was for the dollars for which they were directly accountable to their electors. The money that came from the other levels of governments, primarily in that case from the provincial governments, and to a very minor degree from the federal government, was "found money" from an unending horn of plenty. In our calculations, these funds did not concern us at all-we just calculated, assumed they were there and went on to worry and fuss about the dollars we had to raise from our own municipality, and the impact these would have on the mill rate. I was encouraged, Mr. Speaker, to note that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) have in the past few days made comments supporting this point of view.
A couple of days ago the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair) made reference to the final report of the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons studying the public service of Canada which was made
November 7, 1968	COMMONS
on May 8, 1967. He gave his wholehearted support to its proposal that we should be increasing the pensions paid to our retired civil servants. I would like to add my strong support to his plea. My reasoning here, Mr. Speaker, is precisely the same as it was when I earlier recommended the doubling of the guaranteed income supplement. Our retired citizens worked diligently during their more active years, when economic circumstances were far less attractive than they are today, to build the prosperous society which we all now enjoy. The least we can do now is make certain that these retired Canadians are able to participate fully in the society which they did so much to create.
My final area of comment concerns our athletic endeavours. In the last few weeks all of us have watched with great interest the efforts of our own and other athletes at the Olympics. We are proud of the achievement of our medal winners, but all of us, Mr. Speaker, have a feeling of malaise. We should have done better. Many countries far less well off than ourselves and far smaller in population, such as Czechoslovakia and Kenya, were far more successful. We know that our young athletes are dedicated and competent young people and I think all of us subconsciously feel that we have to dig deeper into the situation to find where we went wrong. Our training facilities are inadequate, we do not possess sufficiently qualified trainers and possibly our athletes did not train hard enough. There are many reasons for our lack of greater success, Mr. Speaker, but it seems to me one area where we could be doing something which would encourage more support of amateur athletics is the relatively minor one of tax relief.
It is my understanding that the encouragement of a particular sport is not considered charitable within the meaning of the Income Tax Act. In my riding we have a vigorous amateur hockey organization and swim club. These groups are faced with fairly substantial on-going expenses for equipment, ice rental, transportation and the many other commitments which are incurred in keeping activities such as these going. We have all watched with admiration the outstanding performance of the United States in the swimming events.
If our young swimmers are going to develop competitively they must get over the border and compete against these young American athletes. There are many interested citizens who are willing to give generously of their time and funds to assist these efforts. I

The Budget-Mr. Skoreyko believe the least we can do is to grant tax relief on the funds which they donate for the support of athletics. I have suggested to some of my friends in these groups that they organize themselves into bodies called "ice worshippers" or "water worshippers", and that part of their religious observances would be to stand around the rink or swimming pool watching their children participate. At least they might then be able to qualify for charitable exemption as a religious organization.
It is absolutely ridiculous that we should decry the lack of athletic achievement when we are not even prepared to permit the people who are willing and eager to support athletic endeavours to deduct their contributions for tax purposes. I urge that the appropriate section of the Income Tax Act be altered as quickly as possible to make such contributions eligible for deduction from taxable income.

Be that as it may, Mr Speaker, at least I was able to identify the hon. member who so eloquently talked about credibility-credibility of the opposition as he said. I wonder if I might be permitted to remind him of a credibility gap in a political party this summer. May I remind him one of the greatest hoaxes ever perpetrated on the Canadian people was engineered this summer on June 25 last. They said nothing to the Canadian people; they promised nothing. In my riding all I heard was "Go Trudeau, go Shewchuk", who was my opponent. This went on all across the country; but indeed when I go back to my riding now I find that an awful lot of people wish he had gone.
I have only two or three minutes left tonight to talk about the budget, Mr. Speaker.
I cannot even begin to criticize it and do an adequate job in that time, and so I hope I have another opportunity to participate in this debate. I want to ask the Minister of Finance how he can justify a 2 per cent increase in personal income tax with a limit of $120? I suggest to him-and he is an accountant-that if he did a little mathematics on his own he could have achieved and indeed exceeded the goal he tried to achieve by charging everybody on earned income, every taxpayer and every wage earner in Canada, one quarter of 1 per cent on total earnings. He would get a lot more money if he had done so. In fact he would have more money than he needed.
I do not understand what justification there is in his concept of fairness or of a just society, when he taxes people who cannot afford to pay 2 per cent on earned income, and at the same time sets a limit of $120. This is something that he thinks fits into this new just society, but it is something that I as a Conservative think is not just. This spring the government promised the Canadian people that it was going to balance the budget in the fall of 1968. To come up with a budget like this is to me tantamount to outright, blatant dishonesty.
I happen to come from the west, Mr. Speaker, where considerable oil development has taken place. I think the minister should take another look at the depletion allowance factor in his budget.
